title: A walkthrough framework: guides are data, and they point at real controls
goal: Build the machinery every tutorial will stand on, and prove it with one real guide. A guide is described as data - a list of steps, each naming a control to point at, what to say about it, and what the person has to do to move on - and the app draws a callout with a pointer aimed at that control, following it as the window moves or resizes. Adding a guide later means adding data, not writing UI. Ship it with one guide working end to end, Take the Tour, so the framework is proven rather than asserted.
notes:
This is the foundation task: nothing else in the tutorials set should start before it lands, and the guide tasks all depend on it.

Reuse what is already there rather than inventing: the app already draws pointer-and-callout chrome for the zoom callout's leader lines (ZoomCalloutOverlayRasterizer, reached from Sources/PhotonzRender/DocumentRenderer.swift:453) and has an overlay family for toasts and popovers (see the overlay work under interaction-foundations). Look at both before writing a third idiom, and say in the audit which one this is built on and why.

The clickthrough mocks are the visual reference the user pointed at: docs/design/mocks/pages (92 pages) and the shared component library at docs/design/mocks/shared/components (tooltip.js, overlays.css, app-patterns.css, redline.css). Conform to docs/design/mocks/shared/UX-PATTERNS.md rather than inventing a callout look.

Keep the step's advance condition HONEST. A step that says "now drag a handle" and advances on a timer is a lie the person will notice. Wire the waiting kind to real editor events, and where an event does not exist yet, say so in the audit and file it rather than faking it.

One more thing worth getting right early because it is expensive later: a guide's copy is product copy, so it obeys the repo's copy rules - no em dashes, no mention of the tooling that built it, short plain human sentences.

---
SHARED CONTEXT for every tutorials task (asked for by the user on 2026-09-12):

The user's words: "I would like a help > tutorials > * set of guides which walks you through basics of various features. Maybe a nice getting started tutorial, maybe a 'building components' walkthrough, etc. ... And maybe a first run experience which lets you get an intro to the app, or just gogogo. Use the design clickthroughs as inspiration, where you have pointers and can point to various parts of the application. Build a nice framework for defining these walkthroughs so that we can extend it over time. I'd like the tutorials system to be well organized and not just a long list of things."

The agreed shape (settled in the intake conversation, 2026-09-12):
- TRACKS, not a flat list. Help > Tutorials holds "Take the Tour" plus one SUBMENU per track, and a Tutorials window is the hub. The tracks are: Basics, Redlining, Looks, Colours & Styles, Building UI, Components, Video.
- A guide is DATA, not code: a Codable value in PhotonzCore describing steps. Adding a guide means adding data to the catalogue, and the menu, the window and the progress list all pick it up with no UI edited. That is the whole point of the framework and the thing that makes it extensible.
- Steps POINT AT REAL UI, clickthrough-style: a callout with a pointer aimed at a named control, not a page of prose.
- Design doc: docs/design/tutorials.md is the source of truth for the framework and the track list, written by the foundation task and extended by the rest.

THE TRAP that will waste a runner's day if it is not read first: the app already has a registry of named UI targets, the playtest harness (playtestControl / playtestField / steady names, Sources/Photonz/Playtest/PanelTarget.swift). It looks like exactly the right thing to reuse and it is NOT USABLE here: it is compiled out of the shipping build (Scripts/build-app.sh defines PHOTONZ_PLAYTEST for the dev and probe variants only, see docs/design/playtest-harness.md, "Who can run it"), and PanelTarget.swift:141 onwards is the no-op stub release actually gets. Tutorials ship to users, so the anchor registry has to be its own thing that is compiled IN for release. Model it on the playtest one - especially the STEADY NAME idea at PanelTarget.swift:126-138, a name taken off the model rather than off the copy, so rewording a label cannot break a guide - but do not depend on it.

Existing surfaces a tutorial entry point must fit with rather than duplicate:
- The Welcome window (Sources/Photonz/Welcome/WelcomeController.swift), first-run permissions setup, re-reachable from the menu-bar menu as "Welcome & Permissions...". It already owns first launch.
- The empty-editor onboarding card (Sources/Photonz/EditorView.swift:590-615): open a file, capture a rectangle, paste an image, blank canvas.
- There is NO Help menu in the app today: EditorCommands.swift declares Capture, Image, Video, Layer and the standard groups, and macOS supplies the default Help menu. Help > Tutorials has to be created.

Queue-driven app work targets the NEXT release unless the task says otherwise (CLAUDE.md), and a Current change is not finished until Next has it.
acceptance: A guide is a Codable value in PhotonzCore with tests: a track, a title, an estimated time, and ordered steps; each step names the control it points at, its copy, which side the callout sits on, and how it advances
A named-anchor registry that is COMPILED INTO THE RELEASE BUILD: a control can be tagged with a stable name and the overlay can ask where it is on screen right now
Anchor names are steady: they come off the model, not off the visible words, so rewording a label cannot break a guide
The callout draws over the app with a pointer at the anchor, and follows it when the window is resized, the panel is scrolled or the layout changes; it never covers the control it is pointing at
Two ways to advance, both working: a Next button, and a step that waits for the person to actually do the thing, then moves on by itself
Back, Skip and close all work at every step, the app is never blocked or modal while a guide runs, and quitting mid-guide loses nothing
A guide can open its own sample document so it never depends on what the person has open, and it never edits their work without saying so first
Take the Tour runs start to finish in the real app, pointing at real controls, and is captured in the audit as a sequence of screenshots
A guide that names an anchor which does not exist fails a test rather than failing a person: a check walks every guide in the catalogue and asserts every anchor resolves
docs/design/tutorials.md written: the data model, the anchor contract, how to add a guide, the track list, and what the framework deliberately does not do
Audit under queue/audits/ with the tour captured step by step, and anything rough filed as a follow-up
